literal: Xianbi again led more than ten thousand men and came again for a decisive battle.
idiomatic: Ma Xianbi rallied another ten thousand men and returned for a final clash.

literal: Ying urged the generals and, as opportunity allowed, divided to strike; he broke them again and again beheaded the rebel general Chen Xiuzhi.
idiomatic: Ying drove his commanders to strike wherever chance offered, routed them once more, and beheaded the Liang general Chen Xiuzhi.

literal: Army commander Wang Mainu separately broke the formation at East Ridge and took five hundred heads.
idiomatic: Army commander Wang Mainu broke the East Ridge line on his own and took five hundred heads.

literal: Dao Gong died of worry; Valiant Cavalry General and acting provincial governor Cai Ling'en again relied on the desperate city, close combat joining day by day.
idiomatic: Dao Gong died of grief; Cai Ling'en, Valiant Cavalry General acting as governor, still held the doomed city as hand-to-hand fighting met day after day.

literal: Jingzong and Xianbi, knowing the city would soon fall, brought their full strength to decisive battle—three clashes in one day—and all were utterly defeated and returned.
idiomatic: Jingzong and Xianbi, seeing the city was lost, threw in every man for three battles in a single day—and were routed each time.

literal: Ling'en's position was desperate and he thereupon surrendered.
idiomatic: Cornered, Ling'en surrendered.

literal: The garrisons of the Three Passes, hearing of it, also abandoned their cities and fled.
idiomatic: Hearing the news, the Three Passes garrisons abandoned their posts and fled.

literal: An edict said: "Knowing the rebel city has fallen and the Three Passes have again been taken, extending might and opening the borders, fame and strategy proclaimed and shaken, public and private all declare peace—truly I am well pleased.
idiomatic: The throne wrote: "The rebel stronghold is down and the Three Passes retaken—might spread across the frontier, your name and plan ringing far; court and country rejoice, and so do I.

literal: The general's deep counsel within, loyal designs raised without, receiving the statutes and raising the banners, fulfilling the temple's plan—though Fang Shu's subduing of the Man and Jing, or Shao Hu's sweeping of the Huai shore, compared with this they are as nothing.
idiomatic: You read the enemy within and laid loyal plans without; under law you raised the standard and fulfilled what the ancestors had plotted. Fang Shu taming the south, Shao Hu clearing the Huai—beside this they are nothing.

literal: Xin Province has newly submitted; you should broadly extend strategy. I trust you will well oversee and inspect, surely making it secure all round; when you have entrusted matters, then return in triumph.
idiomatic: Xinzhou has only just submitted—extend your strategy there, oversee it well until all is secure, entrust what must be entrusted, and then march home in triumph."

literal: Earlier, when Gaozu pacified Hanyang, Ying had merit in battle; restoration of his fief was promised, but in the end he was defeated by Xianda and the matter was shelved.
idiomatic: Earlier, when Gaozu pacified Hanyang, Ying had earned merit and a promise to restore his fief—but Xianda defeated him and the grant was shelved.

literal: In this campaign Emperor Shizong was greatly pleased and restored it; his fief was changed to Prince of Zhongshan with a household of one thousand, and Grand Envoy, Vice Director of the Court for Diplomatic Relations Mu Yanji was sent with credentials to invest him on the spot.
idiomatic: This time Shizong was delighted: the fief was restored as Prince of Zhongshan, one thousand households, and Grand Envoy Mu Yanji of the Court for Diplomatic Relations came with credentials to invest him on the spot.

literal: Ying sent up Cai Ling'en together with Yan's Masters of Writing Attendant Cai Sengrui, Forward Army General and Yiyang Governor Feng Daoyao, Mobile Army General Bao Huaixin, Tianmen Governor Wang Chengbo, Pacify-the-North Staff Major Zong Xiang, Pacify-the-North Staff Adviser Fu Can, Palace Attendant and Pacify-the-North General Cai Daoji, Central Army Major Pang Xiu, and several tens more.
idiomatic: Ying sent up Cai Ling'en and dozens more—among them Yan's attendant Cai Sengrui, Feng Daoyao of Yiyang, Bao Huaixin, Wang Chengbo, Zong Xiang, Fu Can, Cai Daoji, and Pang Xiu.

literal: An edict said: "When we pacify the south of the Yangzi, these may all be released to return.
idiomatic: An edict followed: "When the lands south of the Yangzi are pacified, release them all to go home."

literal: When Ying had returned, Shizong received him in audience, deeply praised and comforted him, and later added one thousand households to his fief.
idiomatic: When Ying returned, Shizong received him, praised him at length, and later added another thousand households.

literal: Xiao Yan sent generals to raid Fei Liang; an edict made Ying bearer of the staff, added Scattered Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary and General Who Pacifies the South, and Area Commander of military affairs on the Yang and Xu routes, with a host of one hundred thousand to suppress them, acting at discretion wherever he went.
idiomatic: Xiao Yan sent troops against Fei Liang; Ying was given the staff, made scattered-cavalier attendant-in-ordinary and General Who Pacifies the South, and commander of Yang and Xu with a hundred thousand men, free to act as he saw fit.

literal: An edict to Ying said: "The rebels' power grows daily; they press Fei Liang, and border generals lagged in planning until it came to this.
idiomatic: The throne told Ying: "The enemy grows stronger by the day and presses Fei Liang; frontier commanders dawdled until we reached this pass.

literal: Therefore this move was made, surely expecting victory—but the army went out and stalled, and Fei Liang has fallen.
idiomatic: We sent you expecting sure victory—yet the host stalled, and Fei Liang is lost.

literal: Hearing it, I am aggrieved and troubled; truly it betrays the original plan.
idiomatic: The news wounds me; it is far from what we intended.

literal: Now the armies gather—one hundred fifty thousand in all. What is your plan for the advance?
idiomatic: Now a hundred fifty thousand stand ready. What is your plan of attack?

literal: When may we expect their destruction—near or far?
idiomatic: How soon will they be destroyed—weeks or months?

literal: In how many days may we reach the enemy?
idiomatic: How many days until you meet the enemy?

literal: Among the measures sure to win, which comes first?
idiomatic: Of the moves that must win, which comes first?

literal: Therefore Infantry Commandant and Acting Director of Palace Secretariat Wang Yun is sent to take your key plans.
idiomatic: I send Infantry Commandant Wang Yun of the Secretariat to hear your plans."

literal: Ying memorialized stating the opportunities.
idiomatic: Ying memorialized on the situation.

literal: He then broke Yinling and beheaded twenty-five of Yan's generals and more than five thousand heads of captives.
idiomatic: He smashed Yinling, beheaded twenty-five of Yan's generals, and took more than five thousand heads.

literal: He again repeatedly broke the rebel armies at Liangcheng, beheading forty-two of their sub-generals; killed, captured, and drowned totaled nearly fifty thousand.
idiomatic: Again and again he broke Yan's armies at Liangcheng, killed forty-two subordinate commanders, and left nearly fifty thousand dead, captured, or drowned.

literal: Yan's Central Army Grand General, Prince of Linchuan Xiao Hong, Right Vice Director of the Masters of Writing Liu Yan, and five other great generals fled along the Huai south;[2] in all thirty myriads of grain were taken.
idiomatic: Yan's Central Army Grand General Xiao Hong of Linchuan, Right Vice Director Liu Yan, and five other great commanders fled south along the Huai;[2] thirty myriads of grain were seized.

literal: An edict comforted Ying: "Knowing you have greatly shattered the whale-like rebels, might shaken across the southern sea, the river shores without dust, the Three Chu rolled in dust, fame reaching the wild corners, the same track beginning—public and private rejoice and comfort; truly it matches my heart.
idiomatic: An edict praised him: "You have shattered the great foe, your might shaking the southern sea; the river shores are clean, the Three Chu lie in dust, your fame reaches the wild marches, and the realm begins to walk one path—court and country rejoice, as I do.

literal: You should ride the momentum and sound, long-drive to Wu and Kuai, cut and pull the remaining embers, and sever their southeast."
idiomatic: Ride that momentum long into Wu and Kuai, cut the last embers, and break their hold on the southeast."

literal: Ying pursued to Matou; Yan's Matou garrison commander abandoned the city and fled, and he thereupon besieged Zhongli.
idiomatic: Ying pursued to Matou; Yan's garrison commander fled, and he besieged Zhongli.

literal: An edict said: "The army has marched long; men and horses are worn and lean; the rebel city is perilous and firm—sudden storming is hard.
idiomatic: An edict said: "The campaign has run long; men and horses are spent; the city is steep and hard to storm.

literal: Between winter and spring it is slightly not the time of advantage; a host of one hundred thousand spends daily without measure.
idiomatic: Winter turning to spring is no season for victory; a hundred thousand mouths cost a fortune each day.

literal: We are plotting a later move—do not wait on this affair.
idiomatic: We mean to strike later—do not hang everything on this siege.

literal: For now you may secretly prepare the Xu defenses as if for a triumphal return, secure the borders and complete the soil, and open display of might and strategy.
idiomatic: Secretly ready the Xu line as if for withdrawal, secure the borders, and show your strategy.

literal: The barbarians of Chu left and right have always been prone to flight; some hide in mountains and lakes, some are hard to control in plunder.
idiomatic: The Chu barbarians left and right have always fled—some into lakes and hills, some to raid where none can hold them.

literal: If there are vicious ringleaders and cunning factions that must be cut down, you may sweep them to clear the borders.
idiomatic: If vicious ringleaders must be cut down, sweep them and clear the frontier.

literal: If they rely on strength and cunning and hold defiles not easy to attack, do not trouble to deploy troops in vain.
idiomatic: If they hold defiles you cannot take without waste, do not waste troops on them.

literal: Near or far for the triumphal return—no further details.
idiomatic: When you come home, near or far, I leave to you."

literal: Ying memorialized: "Your servant received orders to punish crime, my will to destroy the fleeing rebels; measuring the enemy and attacking, I expect from the end of the second month into early third month—by reason it must be taken.
idiomatic: Ying replied: "I came to punish rebels and meant to destroy them; gauging the foe, I set the end of the second month or the start of the third for victory.

literal: But from the first day of this month rain has joined day on day—one may say Heaven goes against men's wishes.
idiomatic: Yet since the first of this month rain has not stopped—Heaven against our wish.

literal: Yet when the king's army marches, movement is not easy; one cannot for a little obstruction and delay at once raise dispute.
idiomatic: Still, a king's army does not turn for a little mud; we must not quarrel over a short delay.

literal: Your servant has also thought deeply.
idiomatic: I have thought hard on this.

literal: If after the third month the sky clears and the ground dries, riding over them will be the rule.
idiomatic: If March brings clear skies and dry ground, we can ride them down.

literal: If rain still joins and we cannot attack, your servant has already raised the Shaoyang bridge higher to guard against flooding assault.
idiomatic: If the rains continue and we cannot attack, I have raised the Shaoyang bridge against flood assault.

literal: Should the waters rise beyond expectation and I fear the bridge will break, your servant has also assigned ship-building; again at Zhongli where the water narrows I am building a pontoon bridge—by mid-third month the bridge will surely be finished.
idiomatic: If the flood breaks the bridge, I am building boats and a pontoon at the narrows by Zhongli—by mid-March it will stand.

literal: Clear weather then storm assault; rain then siege and hold—two plans by land and water, taking success as the limit.
idiomatic: Sun—we storm; rain—we siege: land and water, two plans, success our only measure.

literal: Truly I wish the court especially to open a far-reaching plan, grant a little more indulgence, lend days and months, and not let the work of moving mountains stop halfway.
idiomatic: I beg the court to look far, grant more time, and not abandon a mountain's labor halfway."

literal: An edict said: "The great army camps in the field and has already grown weary long; attack and defense—the principle can be foreseen in advance.
idiomatic: The throne answered: "The host has camped long; attack and defense should be plain.

literal: Recently your memorials repeatedly said victory would be no later than late spring; when I examined the later memorial, again the term was set for the end of early summer.
idiomatic: Your letters promised victory by late spring; the next set midsummer.

literal: That land is steamy and muddy—not fit to linger long.
idiomatic: That country is steam and mud—not fit to linger in.

literal: Though the situation must be taken—that is the general's deep plan;
idiomatic: Taking the city is your deep plan;

literal: troops long deployed, strength exhausted—that is also what the court worries over.
idiomatic: troops long abroad and spent—that is what the court fears.

literal: Therefore Director of Documents Cao Dao is sent to observe the army's condition; when he returns, report each point in full.
idiomatic: I send Director of Documents Cao Dao to see your host; let him report everything."

literal: [3] When Dao returned, Ying still memorialized saying "it can be taken."
idiomatic: [3] When Dao returned, Ying still wrote that the city could be taken.

literal: In the fourth month the waters swelled and broke the bridge; Ying and the generals fled in disarray, and of the soldiers and masses drowned, one or two in ten.
idiomatic: In the fourth month flood broke the bridge; Ying and his officers fled in disorder, and one or two soldiers in ten drowned.

literal: Ying reached Yangzhou and sent envoys to deliver the staff and regalia, marten cap, and seals and cords.
idiomatic: At Yangzhou he sent back his staff, robes, marten cap, and seals.

literal: An edict ordered them delivered to the storehouse.
idiomatic: An edict sent them to the imperial storehouse.

literal: The relevant offices memorialized that Ying's calculations missed the plan and impeached him for death; an edict pardoned death and made him a commoner.
idiomatic: The ministries impeached him for failed strategy and sought death; the throne spared his life and made him a commoner.

literal: Later when Prince Yu of Jingzhao rebelled, Ying's princely title was restored with a fief of one thousand households; he was made bearer of the staff, acting General Who Pacifies the East, and Area Commander of military affairs in Ji Province.
idiomatic: When Prince Yu of Jingzhao rebelled, Ying's title was restored at one thousand households; he was given the staff as acting General Who Pacifies the East and commander of Ji.

literal: Before Ying set out, Ji Province was already pacified.
idiomatic: Before he marched, Ji was already quiet.

literal: At that time Yingzhou Administrator Supervisor Rongzu secretly led Xiao Yan's army; Yiyang answered them, and the garrisons of the Three Passes all held their cities and submitted to Yan.
idiomatic: Yingzhou supervisor Rongzu secretly brought in Xiao Yan's troops; Yiyang joined them, and every Three Passes garrison surrendered.

literal: Yingzhou Inspector Lou Yue defended the city with a closed ring.
idiomatic: Inspector Lou Yue shut the walls and held on.

literal: The people of Xuancheng, Bai Zaosheng and others, killed Yu Province Inspector Sima Yue, held the south of the city, and rebelled.
idiomatic: At Xuancheng, Bai Zaosheng and others killed Inspector Sima Yue, seized the south wall, and rebelled.

literal: Yan's general Qi Gouren led a host to hold Xuancheng.
idiomatic: Yan's Qi Gouren held Xuancheng with an army.

literal: Yue's son had married the Princess of Huayang and was also seized as hostage.
idiomatic: Yue's son, who had married the Princess of Huayang, was taken hostage as well.

literal: An edict made Ying bearer of the staff, Area Commander of the Southern Campaign armies, and acting General Who Pacifies the South, setting out from Runan.
idiomatic: Ying was ordered out from Runan with the staff, command of the southern campaign, and acting General Who Pacifies the South.

literal: Shizong received Ying and said to him: "Lou Yue's soothing and control lost harmony; scales and balance were dark in brief appointment—therefore Ying's people drew in the enemy, pass garrisons fled outward, Yiyang stands lonely and pressed, with the urgency of hanging upside down.
idiomatic: Shizong told him: "Lou Yue lost his grip; the wrong men were posted, so Ying drew in the foe, the passes emptied, and Yiyang hangs by a thread.

literal: The state's Shao Hu of old, might and name long shaken—therefore we bend the prince to take command of the main army in person and sweep clear the foul air.
idiomatic: You are our Shao Hu—your name alone should clear the air. I bend a prince to lead the host and sweep the filth away.

literal: In old times Wei and Huo, because of the Xiongnu, had no year of peace; now the southern border is not quiet—you, prince, may not decline because of repeated toil."
idiomatic: Wei Qing and Huo Qubing knew no peaceful year while the Xiongnu lived; the south is unquiet—you may not refuse because you are weary."

literal: Ying replied: "Your servant's talent is not Han Xin or Bai Qi; my knowledge is dimmer than Sun Wu's or Wu Qi's—only as eldest of the imperial clan I have repeatedly borne the trust of being pushed in the chariot shaft.
idiomatic: Ying answered: "I am no Han Xin or Bai Qi, no Sun Wu or Wu Qi—only as senior prince I have been trusted again and again with the chariot pole.

literal: My strategy shallow and short, losing the statutes and losing the army—I ought to bear the punishment of Zengzi's son in reverse, to answer to the realm.
idiomatic: My plans were shallow; I lost the law and lost the army—I ought to die like Zengzi's son, to answer the world.

literal: Your Majesty's mercy is deep, mindful even of worn sandals, love equal to a bell-ox—your servant may be like Xun Bo, reborn in a bright age, vowing to follow Meng Ke and make repayment the term.
idiomatic: Your mercy is deep—you spare even worn shoes, love me like a sacrificial ox; let me be Xun Bo reborn, follow Mencius, and repay you.

literal: The slight rebels of the passes and Ying—what worth to pacify and destroy? The plan to destroy the rebels is already in your servant's eye; I wish Your Majesty not to trouble the sage worry."
idiomatic: These border fleas are nothing; I already see how to crush them—trouble yourself no further."

literal: Shizong said: "Cutting off their southeast, again clearing Sui and Chu—that is what is hoped from the general.
idiomatic: Shizong said: "I look to you to cut the southeast and clear Sui and Chu again.

literal: Zhongli's one mishap—how could it damage great virtue?
idiomatic: One disaster at Zhongli cannot stain great merit.

literal: Now the prince directs those three armies; I have no worry."
idiomatic: Lead the three armies—I have no fear."

literal: Shizong, because Xing Luan had repeatedly broken Zaosheng, ordered Ying south to Yiyang.
idiomatic: Because Xing Luan had already broken Zaosheng, Shizong sent Ying south to Yiyang.

literal: Ying, because his troops were few, repeatedly memorialized asking for reinforcements; Shizong did not grant it.
idiomatic: Ying, short of men, begged for troops; Shizong refused.

literal: Yet Ying at once joined Xing Luan in dividing troops to attack Xuancheng together; they took it, and then led the army forward.
idiomatic: Yet he joined Xing Luan, took Xuancheng together, and marched on.

literal: When Gouren first held Xuancheng, Yan's Pacify-the-North General Zhang Daoning and others led troops to hold Chucheng; hearing Ying was coming, they abandoned the city and fled south.
idiomatic: While Gouren held Xuancheng, Zhang Daoning held Chucheng; hearing Ying approached, they fled south.

literal: Ying pursued, beheaded Daoning and Yan's Tiger Guard Central Officer Cao Kusheng, and captured their entire host.
idiomatic: Ying ran them down, killed Daoning and Cao Kusheng of the Tiger Guard, and took every man.

literal: Having halted at Yiyang, about to take the Three Passes, Ying calculated: "The Three Passes depend on one another like left and right hands; if one pass is taken, the two passes need not be attacked and are settled.
idiomatic: At Yiyang he planned the Three Passes: "They need each other like two hands—take one, and the other two fall without a fight.

literal: To attack the hard is not as good as attacking the easy; the East Pass is easy to attack—you should first take it, exactly what the Yellow Stone Elder called: battle like wind rising, assault like a river breaking its banks."
idiomatic: Strike the easy, not the hard. The East Pass is weak—take it first, as the Yellow Stone Elder said: fight like wind, strike like a broken river."

literal: Ying feared they would combine strength on the east; he therefore sent Chief Clerk Li Hua with five army groups toward the West Pass to divide their force.
idiomatic: Fearing a concentration in the east, he sent Chief Clerk Li Hua with five columns against the West Pass to split their strength.

literal: He himself supervised the armies toward the East Pass.
idiomatic: He led the main force to the East Pass.

literal: Earlier, Ma Xianbi had sent Cloud-Cavalry General Ma Guang with a host to resist and encamp at Changbo; Army Commander Hu Wenchao separately encamped at Songxian.
idiomatic: Earlier Ma Xianbi had posted Ma Guang at Changbo and Hu Wenchao at Songxian.

literal: When Ying reached Changbo, Ma Guang fled by night into Wuyang; Ying advanced his army to attack.
idiomatic: At Changbo, Ma Guang slipped away by night into Wuyang; Ying followed and besieged him.

literal: Hearing Yan had sent its Champion General Peng Fusheng and Flying Cavalry General Xu Chaoxiu to rescue Wuyang.
idiomatic: Word came that Yan's Champion Peng Fusheng and Flying Cavalry Xu Chaoxiu were marching to relieve Wuyang.

literal: Ying therefore slowed the army and said: "Let them enter this city—I once observed its terrain; it is easy to attack. I take it like picking up something dropped."
idiomatic: Ying slowed his march. "Let them in—I know that ground; it is easy. I will take it as one picks up what was dropped."

literal: The generals did not believe him.
idiomatic: His officers did not believe him.

literal: When Fusheng and the rest had entered Wuyang, Ying pressed the siege; in six days Ma Guang and the rest surrendered.
idiomatic: Once Fusheng was inside, Ying pressed the siege; in six days Ma Guang surrendered.

literal: Thereupon he advanced to strike Huangxian; Yan's Crown Prince Left Guard Leader Li Yuanyi abandoned the city and fled in panic.
idiomatic: He struck Huangxian; Yan's Left Guard Leader Li Yuanyi fled.

literal: He again attacked the West Pass; Yan's Provincial Inspector Ma Xianbi also at once retreated—exactly as Ying had calculated.
idiomatic: He took the West Pass; Ma Xianbi fled at once—just as Ying had foreseen.

literal: In all he captured six of their great generals, twenty sub-generals, seven thousand soldiers, four hundred thousand piculs of grain, and military stores in full measure.
idiomatic: He took six great generals, twenty subordinates, seven thousand men, four hundred thousand piculs of grain, and full stores.

literal: Returning to court, he was appointed Vice Director of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: Back at court he became Vice Director of the Masters of Writing.

literal: In the third year of Yongping, Ying died; he was granted the Eastern Garden secret vessels, one set of court robes, seven hundred bolts of silk, posthumously made Duke of the Secretariat, posthumous title Prince Xianwu.
idiomatic: In Yongping year 3 he died; the court gave secret funeral gear, court robes, seven hundred bolts of silk, posthumous rank as Duke of the Secretariat, and the title Prince Xianwu.

literal: Ying had five sons.
idiomatic: Ying had five sons.

literal: Ying — son — You
idiomatic: Ying's son: You

literal: You, styled Xuanxing, was Eastern Palace Preceptor.
idiomatic: You, courtesy name Xuanxing, served as Eastern Palace Preceptor.
